central_topic: How few comparisons have to be dropped or flipped to change the top-1 or top-k set of a Bradley-Terry leaderboard. The size is measured with a one-step influence (AMIP-style) search verified by exact refits, and is compared across crowdsourced votes (Chatbot Arena 140k), expert and LLM-judge annotations (MT-Bench human and GPT-4 pairs), and sports results (NBA seasons), with synthetic and permutation controls.
core_methods: Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood (ridge-regularized, ties as half wins) fitted to pairwise comparison data
Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP): first-order, influence-function ranking of rows by their effect on the leader-challenger margin
Exponential + binary prefix search with exact refits to verify the smallest perturbation set that changes the ranking
Two perturbation types (dropping rows, flipping outcomes) and two targets (top-1, top-k set)
comparators: Random-subset perturbation baseline (the run reports the log2 size ratio vs random)
Influence functions and leave-one-out / infinitesimal-jackknife approximations
Data-dropping robustness metrics for statistical conclusions (Broderick et al.)
Adversarial manipulation and vote rigging of pairwise rank aggregation and crowdsourced LLM leaderboards
Statistical uncertainty for Bradley-Terry rankings (bootstrap / asymptotic confidence intervals) and top-K ranking theory
benchmarks: MT-Bench human expert judgments and GPT-4 pairwise judgments
FiveThirtyEight NBA historical game records (2014 and 2015 seasons)
Synthetic Bradley-Terry control and permutation control
architectural_shifts: Changing the perturbation model from dropping comparisons to flipping outcomes: flip sets are consistently smaller than drop sets, e.g. Arena top-1 46 flips vs 62 drops
Changing the target from top-1 to the top-k set: on Arena and NBA, top-5 set membership is more fragile than top-1 (Arena 21 vs 62 drops; NBA 1 vs 7 or 16 drops)
Same model responses, different evaluation design: on MT-Bench, human expert and GPT-4 judges give different fragility
result_driven_themes: Large crowdsourced leaderboards can be extremely fragile in relative terms: dropping about 0.05% of Arena-140k votes changes the top-1
Small expert or LLM-judge datasets need a much larger fraction to change the top-1 (about 2.7% for MT-Bench human, about 6% for MT-Bench GPT-4); sports seasons fall in between (about 0.9%)
Influence-guided sets are about 16x smaller than random subsets (mean log2 ratio about 4.0), so the gap between worst-case and average-case sensitivity is large
Fragility depends on the margin between adjacent ranks and on the comparison graph design, not only on dataset size, so a dataset-size-normalized fraction is needed for comparisons across designs
The refined search variants (category-count relinearized knapsack) were never evaluated because of infrastructure failures; the reported sizes are upper bounds from the AMIP search

queries.query: failure modes of approximate maximum influence perturbation when dropping many data points together
queries.rationale: Target method-upper-bound-auditing (high; Method 'What a verified size means', Discussion 'Upper bounds, not minima'). The paper says every size is an upper bound from a one-step influence ordering and that the true minimum may be much smaller. That limitation paragraph cites nothing. This query looks for documented cases where the first-order AMIP ordering misses smaller drop sets. It must not return Broderick2020AnAF, Basu2020InfluenceFI, Koh2017UnderstandingBP, or the Giordano jackknife papers, which are already in the bibliography.

queries.query: exact algorithms and lower-bound certificates for the minimal data-dropping set that overturns a statistical conclusion
queries.rationale: Target method-upper-bound-auditing, the sentence 'Provable auditing is known only in special settings'. That sentence cites only Moitra2022ProvablyAO (low-dimensional OLS). Greedy or exact search methods and lower-bound certificates for worst-case data dropping would back the claim that k* is a hard combinatorial problem and that our sizes are upper bounds. Do not use Moitra2022 again.

queries.query: ranking from pairwise comparisons with a fraction of adversarially corrupted comparisons
queries.rationale: Target related-work-corruption-robust-ranking (Related Work, 'Manipulation and validity of LLM leaderboards'). The flip perturbation stands in for mislabeled or adversarially cast votes. The theory of corruption-robust BTL/rank aggregation is the natural comparator family, and it is absent. The existing Shah2015SimpleRA covers stochastic noise, not adversarial corruption, so do not use it again.

queries.query: data poisoning attack on Bradley-Terry-Luce rank aggregation from pairwise comparisons
queries.rationale: Target related-work-corruption-robust-ranking, anchored at 'Adversarial attacks on rank aggregation have also been analyzed as games between attacker and aggregator'. That sentence currently cites only Ma2022ATO (HodgeRank/spectral). We want 1–2 attack-side papers on BTL-type aggregators that sit next to our drop and flip sets. Exclude Ma2022ATO and Min2025ImprovingYM, which are already cited.

queries.query: Bradley-Terry paired comparison model for rating sports teams from game results
queries.rationale: Target method-data-sports-design (Method, 'Data and protocol', the sentence that models each NBA game as a comparison between two teams). The NBA design produces the count-scale finding, yet the only sports citation is Elo1978 (chess). A BT or paired-comparison sports-rating reference would motivate treating games as BT comparisons.

queries.query: statistical rating models for professional basketball team strength and game outcome prediction
queries.rationale: Target method-data-sports-design, second search topic. It looks for a basketball- or team-sport-specific rating reference that supports using NBA seasons as a dense, balanced-schedule design. Use it only if the previous query does not return a suitable team-sport paper. Add at most one citation.
